proxy_language: Proto-Indo-European (late/Northwest-European dialect zone) as a deliberately weak proxy; alternative would be Proto-Uralic, rejected for primary use
proxy_rationale: The Swiderian (c. 11,000-9,000 BCE, Final Palaeolithic/early Mesolithic reindeer-hunting tool-making culture of the Polish-Belarusian-Baltic sandy plains, successor to Federmesser/Creswellian-type groups) is known only from stone tools (tanged points) and sites. No language can be linked. The region's later languages were Baltic and Finnic/Saami (Uralic) and, before them, unknown Mesolithic tongues, and the Old European hydronymy (Krahe) in the Baltic basin is traditionally read as an early Indo-European layer. For a game, PIE reconstruction notation gives a principled, phonotactically coherent system but with no claim of historical identity. The Swiderian language was almost certainly not PIE (PIE is conventionally dated to c. 4500-3500 BCE) and is not recoverable; treat this as a naming convention only. Use reconstructed roots (asterisked) and never present results as attested.
phonology: Conventional PIE (Fortson/Ringe/Beekes notation). Stops: *p *t *k *kw (labiovelar; palatovelar *k' and plain *k collapsed to k for simplicity), *b *d *g *gw, aspirates *bh *dh *gh *gwh (collapsed to bh dh gh for the game). Fricative *s. Nasals *m *n. Liquids *r *l. Glides *y *w. Laryngeals h1 h2 h3 (written h1/h2/h3 or collapsed to h). Vowels *e *o *a (rare), long variants, plus syllabic resonants. No real attested Swiderian phonology exists.
phonotactics: Roots are normally monosyllabic of shape (s)C(C)eC(C) with e-grade; maximum one stem vowel e/o. Initial clusters: s+stop (st, sp, sk), stop+liquid/glide (pr, tr, kr, pl, kl, tw, kw), s+resonant. Final clusters limited: -rt, -nt, -st, -ks. Syllabic resonants (r, l, m, n) may serve as nuclei between consonants. Words in game use: CV(C), CVC, CVCV(C) shapes, vowels e/o/a/i/u. No voiced aspirate + voiceless stop adjacency (bh-t, gh-t etc. assimilate). Roots do not begin and end with plain voiced stops of the same type (the b-e-d / d-e-g constraint).
orthography: Reconstruction notation in plain Latin letters without asterisk in names: h for laryngeals (h1/h2/h3 simplified to h), kw gw gwh for labiovelars, bh dh gh for voiced aspirates, y w for glides, long vowels as doubled letters or macrons (e.g. ee/oo or e/o with macron). Syllabic resonants not marked. Case/ending vowels written -os, -om, -a, -i, -u, -es.
morphology: Root + suffix structure: root (monosyllabic) + thematic vowel -e-/-o- + case ending. Nominative -s (masc/fem), neuter -m / zero; accusative -m, genitive -s/-es/-os/-syo (thematic), locative -i, ablative -(o)s/-ed, instrumental -(e)h1. Collective/feminine -eh2 (-a). Derivation: -ti- (action nouns), -tor- (agent), -yo- (adjective/relational), -mn (result/instrument), -tro-/-dhlo- (tool nouns), -ent-/-went- (possessor), -ko- (adjective), -ro- (adjective). Reduplication used in presents and some nouns (e.g. *kwekwlo-).
compounding: Compounds are head-final determinative compounds: modifier stem + head noun, with a linking -o- (e.g. *ph2tr-o-... or *newo-bhrh2tr-). Possessive (bahuvrihi) compounds also head-final: 'X-having'. Genitive phrase 'Y of X': head noun + genitive of X, or compound X-o-Y. Agent names: noun + -tor / -o- + root, e.g. 'deer-hunter' = *g'hwer-o-wiHkwo. For game: 'X of Y' as Y-genitive after head or compound Y-o-X; 'Y-maker' as Y + -o- + root-agent.
noun_phrase_order: Adjective + noun, genitive + noun in compounds; in free syntax PIE order was flexible (SOV default); adjectives agree in case/number/gender; genitive before head noun is the default for the game. Demonstrative before noun.
sources: Fortson, Indo-European Language and Culture (2nd ed. 2010)
Schild & Wiktor, Late Pleistocene Swiderian culture overview (Polish archaeological literature, e.g. Schild 1975)
notes: Swiderian has no linguistic evidence at all; this is a naming proxy. The game's placeholder names (Xubayir wunis; Wudik puworwa) contain letters (x, b-ay-ir) and cluster types not allowed in the proxy. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word since PIE reconstructions are not Goidelic; avoid accidental matches such as 'mena' or 'bo'.
